Do copper bullets offer the same performance to hunters as lead bullets?

Copper bullets are really lead projectiles with a copper jacket. This wasn't always necessary until the development of High velocity calibers. The high velocity created a bullet that spun a lot faster than a lead bullet. This centrifugal force caused the lead bullet to deform, (essentially becoming shorter and bigger around) which caused some erratic flight characteristics. Also lead projectiles fired at high velocity tended to leave lead fouling in the bore. This over time reduced the effectiveness of the rifling and decreased the diameter of the bore.

I load a 173 grain lead cast projectile for my .30 cal. (.30-06 and 7.62X51 mm) These lead casts are used over a 11 grains of Unique Pistol powder. Gives me about 1400 fps. Even cycles my M1A can you imagine that. All my cast loads are gas checked to provide better sealing and to cut down on Lead fouling. These loads are quite accurate but should be limited to 100 yds or less. They have the trajectory of a brick. To shoot Lead cast at a higher velocity you need to move down to a slower burning powder, like IMR 4198. However you should never attempt to shoot lead casts at over 2000 fps. However the most accurate loads for lead cast projectiles is a the lowest velocity.

As for effectiveness for hunting just look at the statistics for wounds during the American Civil War. Even light wounds requited the amputation of limbs, and if you were hit in the abdomen or chest cavity it was a very slow and painful death. (The reason why you see the photos of Dead Soldiers with their clothing all in disarray is because the were opening their shirts to see where they were hit before the died) This is why hollow point and lead projectiles and hollow Cavity projectiles were banned under the protocols of the Hague Convention of 1899 which predates the Geneva conventions.

There was a very completed analysis of the military use of Lead Projectiles authored by the International Committee of the Red Cross and submitted to the United Nations for action. The report was approved for an addenda to the Laws of Land Warfare by the General Assembly of the United Nations in 1973.
